title: Switch Statements
description: Master C# switch statements and switch expressions, including traditional case syntax, modern expression-bodied forms, and advanced pattern matching with type, relational, and logical patterns introduced in C# 7 through C# 12.

data.text: When you need to compare a single value against many possible outcomes, a long chain of if-else if statements becomes hard to read and maintain. The switch statement exists to solve exactly this problem: it lets you express multi-way branching clearly and concisely. Over the years, C# has dramatically evolved switch from a simple case-matching statement into a powerful expression with full pattern matching support.

A switch statement evaluates an expression (called the switch expression) and compares its result against a list of case labels. When a match is found, the code in that case block runs. If no case matches and a default block exists, the default runs. C# requires a break, return, throw, or goto at the end of each case block to prevent fall-through between cases — this is a deliberate safety feature that prevents subtle bugs.

terms.definition: The value inside the switch parentheses, evaluated once at the beginning.
A specific value the switch expression is compared against. Declared with the case keyword.
The fallback case that runs when no other case matches. Declared with the default keyword.
When execution continues into the next case block without a break. C# prevents this by requiring explicit jumps.
A syntax rule that describes a shape of data. Pattern matching allows case labels to be more than simple constant values.
A modern expression-bodied form of switch introduced in C# 8 that returns a value directly.

    Case1 -- No --> Case2{Matches case 2?}

    Exec1 --> Break1[break / return / throw]
    Exec2 --> Break2[break / return / throw]
    Exec3 --> Break3[break / return / throw]
    ExecDefault --> BreakDefault[break / return / throw]
    Break1 --> EndSwitch
    Break2 --> EndSwitch
    Break3 --> EndSwitch
    BreakDefault --> EndSwitch

data.text: The traditional switch statement has been part of C# since version 1.0. It uses the switch keyword followed by an expression in parentheses, then a series of case and default blocks enclosed in braces. Each case label declares a constant value to compare against. Multiple case labels can point to the same block by omitting code between them — this is called case fall-through by design, and it is the one form of fall-through C# intentionally allows.

Every case block must end with an unconditional jump statement: break, return, throw, or goto case. This is not optional. If you forget it, the compiler will produce an error. This rule prevents the accidental fall-through bugs common in languages like C or JavaScript.

data.text: Introduced in C# 8.0, switch expressions are a modern, expression-bodied alternative to the traditional switch statement. Instead of assigning a value inside case blocks and breaking, a switch expression produces a value directly. The syntax uses the => (lambda) arrow after each case, and the entire construct returns a value that can be assigned or returned immediately. This makes the code more concise and functional in style.

Switch expressions also introduce the discard pattern _, which replaces the default keyword. They support the or pattern (combining multiple matches), and they work seamlessly with all the pattern types introduced in later C# versions. Because they are expressions, they can be used in variable declarations, method returns, and anywhere else a value is expected.

data.text: Pattern matching extends far beyond matching exact constant values. Starting with C# 7.0 and expanding through C# 12, patterns let you describe the shape or range of a value you want to match. Relational patterns like >, <, >=, <= let you match numeric ranges. Logical patterns let you combine patterns with and, or, and not. Type patterns let you match on an object's runtime type.

data.title: When to Use Switch vs if-else-if
data.text: Use switch when you are comparing one expression against many discrete values or patterns. Use if-else-if when conditions are unrelated boolean checks. If you find yourself using more than three else if clauses, switch is usually the clearer choice.

cards.title: Traditional Switch Statement
cards.description: The original statement-based switch. Uses case and default blocks with break statements.
pros: Familiar to developers from other languages
Supports statements with multiple lines per case
cons: Does not return a value directly

cards.title: Switch Expression
cards.description: Modern expression-bodied form. Uses case => result syntax and returns a value.
pros: Can be used inline anywhere a value is expected
cons: Each case must be a single expression
Discard _ may be unfamiliar to beginners

data.text: As you advance, you will encounter property patterns, positional patterns, and list patterns. Property patterns let you match on object properties, like checking if a Person object has an Age over 18. Positional patterns deconstruct tuples or types with Deconstruct methods. List patterns (C# 11+) let you match specific sequences inside arrays or lists.

items.question: Can a switch expression throw an exception?
items.answer: Yes. If you use throw in a case arm of a switch expression, it will throw at runtime if that arm is matched. This is useful for exhaustive matching — if you forget a case, the compiler may warn you, or you can use throw as a safety net.

items.question: What is the difference between switch and switch expression?
items.answer: A switch statement runs side effects (writes to console, modifies variables). A switch expression produces and returns a value. If you need a value back, use switch expression. If you need to run statements, use switch statement.

items.question: Why does C# require break in switch statements?
items.answer: C# prevents accidental fall-through by requiring an explicit jump statement at the end of every case block. The only allowed fall-through is when multiple case labels point to the same block with no code between them. This design eliminates a common source of bugs found in languages like C.

items.question: What version of C# do I need for switch expressions?
items.answer: Switch expressions require C# 8.0 or later, which is available in .NET Core 3.0+, .NET 5+, and .NET Standard 2.1+. If you are targeting an older framework, you must use the traditional switch statement.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Switch statements compare one expression against multiple case values
Every case block in a traditional switch must end with break, return, or throw
Switch expressions (C# 8+) return a value directly using case => result syntax
The _ discard replaces default in switch expressions
Property patterns match on object properties in C# 8+
Prefer switch expressions over long if-else-if chains for clarity
data.takeaway: Switch constructs are the cleanest way to handle multi-way branching. Modern C# switch expressions with pattern matching combine conciseness with expressive power, making your branching logic both shorter and easier to read.
